- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slope or cap upward bias.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.7) and price is rising, model often over-optimistically extrapolates; cap forecast growth or introduce early mean reversion.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; apply decay factor or reduce forecast slope for next 3–5 days.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed (e.g., alternating 0.2–0.8), model often fails to capture mean reversion; use sentiment-weighted moving average or adjust forecast toward recent 7-day average.
- If true outcome shows strong downward trend after forecast peak, model often fails to anticipate reversal; add sentiment decay penalty or reduce forecast amplitude post-spike.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to underestimate volatility in sentiment-driven markets; increase forecast variance or add sentiment-based volatility multiplier.
- If sentiment history shows recent negative sentiment (e.g., 0.1–0.4) and price is falling, model often underestimates further decline; adjust downward bias by 5–10% of current forecast.
